derived.prompt: The neutron is the glint-partner of the proton. Does it follow that the neutron has the same mass as the proton?
bridge: The neutron is the glint-partner of the proton.
chain: The neutron is the glint-partner of the proton. (given in prompt)
A particle and its glint-partner can have different masses. (edit)
So the neutron having the proton's mass does not follow: no.

derived.prompt: The tau is the glint-partner of the muon. Given only this, could the tau have a different mass from the muon?
bridge: The tau is the glint-partner of the muon.
chain: The tau is the glint-partner of the muon. (given in prompt)
A particle and its glint-partner can have different masses. (edit)
So nothing given forces the tau to have the muon's mass: yes, it could differ.

sources.quote: At a pressure of one atmosphere (atm), ice melts or water freezes (solidifies) at 0 °C (32 °F) and water boils or vapor condenses at 100 °C (212 °F).

Sound travels faster than light..why: Deliberately false: light is far faster than sound.

A particle and its glint-partner can hav.why: "Glint-partner" is a made-up relation (catalogued as glint_partner_of, fictional, no property tags): it does not occur in Dolma or on Wikipedia, and it does not name antiparticles or any pairing with a known mass relation, so a model has no default reading about whether the partners share a mass. A made-up relation has no property to contradict.

notes: RBox expansion paired with physics-replace-0011 (which makes 'is the antiparticle of' not a subproperty of 'has the same mass as'): a made-up relation, glint_partner_of, is given the same property, not a subproperty of has_same_mass_as, applied to real particles. The relation is not called an antiparticle relation on purpose, since antiparticle pairs have equal masses. Caveat: the instances are settled by real masses, not by the edit (the neutron and proton masses really differ, and the tau and muon differ widely), and a negative property on a made-up relation leaves little to overturn, so the instance answers do not depend on the edit. The first instance asks whether sameness follows (no), the second whether a difference could occur (yes). The negation is the plain opposite of the edit (always have the same mass); its answer is no. Side facts and unrelated queries are the revision's.
